messages.content: My landlord in a state that has adopted rules based on the Model Tenancy Act wants me to pay 4 months' rent as a residential security deposit, saying it's negotiable. Is that legal?

No, this exceeds what's permitted. Under Section 11 of the Model Tenancy Act, 2021, the security deposit for residential premises cannot exceed 2 months' rent — this cap is a statutory ceiling, not something that becomes negotiable by mutual agreement, since the whole point of the provision is to protect tenants from being pressured into oversized deposits. If your state has actually adopted this cap into its own tenancy law or rules, a demand for 4 months' rent as deposit would not be legally enforceable, and you could raise this with the Rent Authority set up under the state's tenancy framework if the landlord insists. If your state hasn't formally adopted the Model Tenancy Act framework, this specific cap may not yet be legally binding there, and you'd need to check whether your state has its own separate rent control law addressing deposit limits instead.
A builder in Dehradun changed my flat's possession date without my consent, and I paid ₹1,100,000 so far. Can I get out of the deal?

Yes. Under Section 18(1) of the Real Estate (Regulation and Development) Act, 2016, if the builder unilaterally changes the agreed possession date, you have the right to withdraw from the project. You must exercise this within 45 days of the changed date being communicated (or of the original committed date passing without possession), and on withdrawal, the builder is required to refund the full ₹1,100,000 you've paid, along with interest at the rate notified by the Dehradun state's RERA authority. Alternatively, instead of withdrawing, you can choose to remain in the project and claim monthly interest compensation for the delay until possession is actually handed over. Either way, you should file your complaint with the relevant state RERA authority to enforce this right, since the builder is unlikely to volunteer the refund without a formal demand or complaint.
A cheque for ₹12,000 that someone gave me to repay a debt bounced due to insufficient funds. What are my legal options?

This is governed by Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881. First, you (or your lawyer) must send the drawer a written legal notice within 30 days of learning the cheque bounced, demanding payment of the ₹12,000. The drawer then has 15 days from receiving that notice to pay up; if they don't, your cause of action for filing a criminal complaint begins on the 16th day, and you generally have 1 month from then to file the complaint in the appropriate Magistrate's court (delay beyond this needs a condonation application with sufficient cause shown). If convicted, the drawer faces imprisonment up to 2 years, a fine up to twice the cheque amount (up to ₹24,000 here), or both — and courts often lean toward ordering payment of compensation (up to the cheque amount or more) rather than jail time, especially if the drawer is willing to pay. The offence is bailable, compoundable, and non-cognizable, meaning the matter can be settled between you and the drawer at any stage of the proceedings.
A woman's mother wants to know exactly what reliefs the Magistrate can grant if she files on her daughter's behalf under Section 12.

Section 12 lets the mother, as someone acting on the aggrieved woman's behalf, present the application, and the Magistrate can then grant one or more reliefs in the same proceeding: a protection order under Section 18 restraining further violence, a residence order under Section 19 protecting her right to stay in the shared household, monetary relief under Section 20 for expenses and losses, a custody order under Section 21 if children are involved, and compensation for injuries under Section 22. Before deciding, the Magistrate must consider any Domestic Incident Report from a Protection Officer or service provider, and is expected to dispose of the application within 60 days of the first hearing under Section 12(5).
I'm a woman whose father passed away before 2005. My brothers say I have no claim to our ancestral property since the law changed after his death. Are they right?

No, they're very likely wrong on the current law. The Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005 rewrote Section 6 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 so that a daughter becomes a coparcener 'by birth' in a Mitakshara joint Hindu family, with the same rights and liabilities as a son in the ancestral (coparcenary) property. For years there was genuine confusion about whether this applied only if the father was still alive on 9 September 2005 (the date the amendment took effect) -- the Supreme Court gave conflicting signals in Prakash v. Phulavati (2016) and Danamma v. Amar (2018). This was finally and authoritatively settled by a three-judge bench in Vineeta Sharma v. Rakesh Sharma (2020): a daughter's right to be a coparcener arises by birth and does NOT depend on her father being alive when the 2005 amendment came into force. The main exception the law carves out is for any partition, testamentary disposition, or alienation of the property that was already validly completed before 20 December 2004 -- that isn't reopened. If your father's estate hasn't been formally and validly partitioned before that date, you generally have an equal coparcenary share alongside your brothers. This is general information; a property lawyer should review your family's specific documents (any past partition deed, will, etc.) before you act.

This clause appears in an agreement I was given: "The party committing breach agrees to indemnify and hold harmless the other party against all third-party losses, costs, and attorney fees." What does it mean in practical terms?

Plain Meaning: The clause states: "The party committing breach agrees to indemnify and hold harmless the other party against all third-party losses, costs, and attorney fees." Explanation: This is an indemnity clause. Under Indian law, indemnity protects the promisee from loss caused by the conduct of the promisor or any third party. Unlike ordinary damages under Section 73 which require proof of actual foreseeable loss, an indemnity obligation is triggered upon accrual of liability. Practical Advice: Read this in the context of the entire document, especially definitions, cure periods, and exception clauses.
What is the correct legal procedure someone from my hometown should follow regarding revoking a conditional gift for failure to maintain under Indian law?

Section 23(1) of the Senior Citizens Act, 2007 provides that where a senior citizen transfers property on condition the transferee provide basic amenities and physical needs, and the transferee fails to do so, the transfer can be declared void by the Maintenance Tribunal.
In Maharashtra, if someone is caught drunk driving a second time after already being convicted once, what happens?

For a subsequent offence under Section 185 of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988, the punishment is more severe: imprisonment up to 2 years, a fine up to ₹15,000, or both — this applies uniformly across India, including in Maharashtra, since the Motor Vehicles Act is a central law. License suspension is also more likely to be for a longer duration on a repeat conviction, and courts generally treat a second conviction far more strictly than a first one, since the law's 2019 amendment specifically raised penalties to deter repeat offenders.
An artist friend of mine wants to understand how long copyright protection lasts. Could you walk through what applies to them?

The Copyright Act, 1957's 60-year term (extended from the original 50 years by a 1992 amendment, to bring it in line with international norms) applies to the individual work itself, not to the author's entire body of work as a unit — each work has its own copyright term running from that author's death (or the last surviving joint author's death). In practice, this means your artist friend can't assume a work is still protected just because it feels recent — an author who died before roughly 1966 would already have works in the public domain in India, since more than 60 years have passed.
If someone in my apartment complex is affected by anticipatory bail, what should they know about their legal rights or obligations?

The BNSS, 2023 shifted anticipatory bail from CrPC Section 438 to its own Section 482. The substance of the remedy is unchanged: someone who reasonably apprehends arrest for a non-bailable offence can ask the Sessions Court or High Court to direct that they be released on bail if arrested. One statutory exception under Section 482(4) blocks this route in cases of rape of a girl under sixteen or gang rape of a woman under eighteen. In practice, practically, this gives that person a legal route to avoid arrest altogether while the case proceeds, provided the underlying offence isn't one of those excluded under Section 482(4).
Can you explain what Indian law says about hit-and-run accident compensation, for a friend's mother?

The Motor Vehicles Act's hit-and-run compensation scheme, in force since April 2022, guarantees Rs 2 lakh to the family in case of death and Rs 50,000 for grievous injury, paid out of the Motor Vehicles Accident Fund even if the driver responsible is never identified. Accepting this payout, however, closes the door on separately approaching the Motor Accident Claims Tribunal for a higher amount. In practice, your friend's mother should be aware that accepting the Rs 2 lakh or Rs 50,000 payout under this scheme generally means giving up the right to separately claim a larger amount before the Motor Accident Claims Tribunal.
How do the missing details in 'A client gave me a cheque that bounced, and I want to recover the money.' affect the calculation of limitation period?

Limitation Calculation: Under the Limitation Act and Banking and Financial Law statutes, limitation runs from specific trigger events: (1) The date on the bank return memo; (2) Whether statutory demand notice was dispatched within 30 days of receiving the memo; (3) Whether 15 days elapsed without payment. Analysis: Without knowing the exact dates of cause of action and notice, assessing whether the claim is subsisting or barred is impossible.
If someone refuses to take a breathalyser test when stopped by police in Ladakh, is that treated the same as failing it?

Yes. Under Section 185 of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988, as applied uniformly across India including in Ladakh since this is a central law, refusal to undergo a breath test is generally treated as a positive reading for the purpose of prosecution — courts and traffic police treat refusal as an aggravating factor rather than a way to avoid the charge. If prosecuted and convicted for a first offence, the punishment is imprisonment up to 6 months, a fine up to ₹10,000, or both, with a subsequent offence attracting up to 2 years' imprisonment and a fine up to ₹15,000. The legal limit remains 30 mg of alcohol per 100 ml of blood, and beyond the breathalyser, police can rely on a blood test under Section 204 of the Act if a breath test is refused or inconclusive.
A person i met recently is dealing with a situation involving first conviction for simple theft. What does Indian law say about this?

This is theft under Section 303 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), 2023, the successor to Section 378 IPC. For a first conviction, Section 303(2) prescribes imprisonment of either description for up to three years, a fine, or both.
Under Indian law, what are the rules regarding filing a domestic violence complaint?

Under Section 12 of the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005, an aggrieved person, a Protection Officer, or someone acting on her behalf can file an application before a Magistrate seeking relief for domestic violence.
The police station near me is refusing to register an FIR for a theft I reported, saying they'll 'look into it first.' Is that legal?

No -- under Section 173(1) of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), 2023 (in force from 1 July 2024, replacing Section 154 CrPC), registration of an FIR is mandatory the moment the information given discloses a cognizable offence like theft. The Supreme Court settled this in Lalita Kumari v. State of U.P. (2014): police cannot refuse registration to first 'verify' the complaint's merit. If the officer-in-charge still refuses, you can send the complaint in writing by post to the Superintendent of Police, who must either investigate personally or direct a subordinate to register the FIR. You can also approach the Magistrate under the BNSS provision equivalent to old Section 156(3) CrPC to direct registration. Note: for some categories of cognizable offences punishable with 3 to 7 years' imprisonment, Section 173(3) BNSS does allow a time-bound preliminary inquiry (with DSP-level permission, ordinarily within 14 days) before registration -- but plain theft reported with clear facts doesn't fall into that carve-out. This is general information, not legal advice for your specific case.
What are the sequential procedural steps for initiating statutory action for cheque dishonour in India?

The process for initiating statutory action for cheque dishonour under Banking and Financial Law requires compliance with established steps: Step 1: Present cheque within 3 months validity and obtain bank return memo. Step 2: Dispatch formal statutory demand notice within 30 days of receiving return memo. Step 3: Grant the drawer 15 days from receipt of notice to make payment. Step 4: If unpaid, file criminal complaint before Judicial Magistrate within 30 days thereafter. Formats, fee schedules, and limitation periods must be verified with the official forum rules.
How many days do I have to file my case? Just give me a number.

Limitation periods in India vary quite a lot depending on the type of case -- a consumer complaint (2 years), a motor accident claim (no fixed limit), a civil suit for a contract (often 3 years, but this varies by claim type under the Limitation Act), and criminal complaints (which vary by offence) all have different rules. Giving you one number without knowing what kind of case this is would likely be wrong. What's the case about?
Can you explain what Indian law says about gratuity owed after leaving a job, for a colleague at work?

Five years of continuous service is the general eligibility threshold for gratuity under the 1972 Act, but this bar disappears entirely if the employee's service ends because of death or disablement — their nominee or they themselves become entitled regardless of tenure. The formula for full-time employees is last drawn wages divided by 26, multiplied by 15, multiplied by the number of completed years of service, subject to the Rs 20 lakh statutory cap. In practice, this means your colleague doesn't need five years of service at all if the separation was due to death or disablement — that eligibility bar is waived entirely in those situations.
A friend's mother brought up whether a small business needs to register for GST recently — what should I tell them about the legal side of it?

The turnover figure that matters for GST registration is 'aggregate turnover' — which is broader than just taxable sales, and includes exempt supplies, exports, and inter-state supplies too, all computed PAN-India across every branch of the business, not per state. So a business might look like it's under the Rs 40 lakh goods threshold on taxable sales alone but actually be over it once exempt and export turnover is added in. In practice, this means your friend's mother isn't required to register below the applicable threshold, but doing so voluntarily can still make sense if your friend's mother wants to claim input tax credit on purchases.

Under Section 89 of the Hindu Marriage Act, is a mutual consent divorce automatically void if the couple reconciles and starts living together again during the six-month waiting period, without formally withdrawing the petition?

I'm not able to verify that Section 89 of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 deals with mutual consent divorce or automatic voidance during the cooling-off period, and I don't want to give you an answer based on an unconfirmed section number — the Hindu Marriage Act's substantive provisions on divorce by mutual consent are set out in Section 13B, not Section 89. What I can say generally is that under Section 13B(2), the second motion requires the parties to affirmatively state that consent has not been withdrawn; simply resuming cohabitation without formally withdrawing the petition would likely be relevant evidence but the precise procedural consequence would depend on how the specific family court handles it. Please have the exact section and effect verified against the current bare act or a family law practitioner rather than relying on the section number in your question.
A factory near my village has been discharging untreated effluent into the river for the past 3 months. Can this be taken to the National Green Tribunal, and is there a time limit?

Yes, this is squarely the kind of matter the National Green Tribunal handles. Under Section 14 of the National Green Tribunal Act, 2010, the NGT has jurisdiction over all civil cases involving a substantial question relating to the environment, arising from enactments listed in Schedule I to the Act (which covers major pollution-control and environment-protection laws). Section 14(3) requires that the application be filed within 6 months from the date the cause of action first arose, though the Tribunal can condone a delay of up to a further 60 days if satisfied there was sufficient cause. Given your timeline, you're well within this window, so it's worth filing soon rather than waiting, since the clock doesn't pause. The Tribunal aims to dispose of matters within 6 months of filing and isn't bound by the ordinary Code of Civil Procedure, which usually makes it faster than a regular civil suit.
A friend's mother is dealing with a situation involving a 16-18 year old accused of a serious crime. What does Indian law say about this?

Offences under the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015 are split into petty (up to 3 years), serious (3 to 7 years), and heinous (7 years or more) categories. Only the heinous category, and only for children between 16 and 18, opens the door to trial as an adult, following a preliminary capacity assessment by the Juvenile Justice Board — a child below 16, regardless of the offence, cannot be tried as an adult under this Act. In practice, this means your friend's mother shouldn't assume adult trial is automatic just because the offence sounds serious — the specific offence has to carry a real statutory minimum of seven years, not just a high maximum.
My neighbour asked me about getting married under the Special Marriage Act — what's the actual legal position under Indian law?

Under Sections 5 to 7 of the Special Marriage Act, 1954, a couple wanting a civil marriage must first give written notice to the Marriage Officer of the district where at least one of them has lived for the preceding 30 days. The Marriage Officer then publishes this notice for 30 days, during which anyone can object on specific statutory grounds (such as bigamy or a prohibited relationship); if no valid objection is raised, the marriage can be solemnised after that period. In practice, for your neighbour, the residency requirement means the notice has to be filed with the Marriage Officer of a district where one of them has actually lived for the preceding 30 days — not just anywhere convenient.
If a relative going through a difficult time is affected by being laid off or retrenched from a job, what should they know about their legal rights or obligations?

Section 25F of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 requires an employer to satisfy three conditions before retrenching a workman who has completed at least one year of continuous service: one month's written notice (or wages in lieu of notice), retrenchment compensation equal to 15 days' average pay for every completed year of continuous service, and notice served on the appropriate government authority. In practice, in your relative's case, it's worth checking the average pay calculation carefully, since retrenchment compensation is meant to be 15 days per completed year, not a token lump sum the employer sets unilaterally.
How does Indian law actually treat eligibility for mutual consent divorce, and what is the specific statutory basis for it?

Section 13B(1) of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 allows a joint divorce petition where spouses have lived separately for at least one year, cannot live together, and mutually agree to dissolve the marriage.
A client wants to know what kind of relief she can ask for besides a protection order. What does the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005 provide?

Section 12 read with the later chapters lets her seek several kinds of relief in a single application: protection orders (Section 18) restraining further violence, residence orders (Section 19) securing her right to stay in the shared household, monetary relief (Section 20) covering expenses, medical costs, and loss of earnings, custody orders (Section 21) for children, and compensation for injuries caused by the abuse (Section 22). All of these can be sought together, rather than filing separate proceedings for each.
I run a small consulting outfit in Andhra Pradesh with turnover close to ₹1,700,000 a year. Do I cross the GST registration threshold?

Under Section 22 of the CGST Act, 2017, the registration threshold for a supplier of services in Andhra Pradesh is ₹2,000,000, and since your turnover of ₹1,700,000 is below that, registration isn't mandatory yet — though you can register voluntarily under Section 25(3) if you want to claim input tax credit or your buyers need GST invoices from you. Keep in mind certain activities trigger compulsory registration under Section 24 regardless of turnover, such as inter-state supply or selling through e-commerce platforms.
What are the practical consequences under Indian law if the issue of police assistance in implementing an order isn't handled correctly?
Section 19(5) of the PWDV Act, 2005 lets the Magistrate direct the local police officer-in-charge to assist in implementing a residence or protection order.
My company received an arbitral award in a licensing dispute exactly 3 months ago today. Is today still within the deadline to challenge it?

Yes, today is your deadline day under the strict reading of Section 34(3) of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, which requires the application to set aside the award to be filed within 3 months from the date you received it. Courts treat this 3-month period as running from the date of actual receipt (not delivery, which can be a distinct legal concept), and computing 'three months' generally means the corresponding date in the third month, not a fixed count of 90 days. Since you are exactly at the 3-month mark, you should file your application today if at all possible; if you miss today, you would need to rely on the additional 30-day condonable extension under the proviso to Section 34(3), which requires showing sufficient cause for not filing on time — so don't take the risk if you can file now.
What is the correct legal procedure a distant relative should follow regarding withdrawing consent before the decree under Indian law?
Either spouse can withdraw consent to a mutual consent divorce under Section 13B(2) at any point before the decree is passed, halting the mutual-consent proceeding.
Does Section 45 of the RTI Act 2005 allow the government to charge unlimited fees for large information requests?

I'm not able to verify a Section 45 in the RTI Act, 2005 dealing with fees. The RTI Act, 2005 does not have a section by that number covering this topic as far as I can confirm — fee structures for RTI applications are typically set out in the Central or State RTI Rules made under the Act, not directly in a specific numbered section allowing unlimited fees. Please verify the applicable Rules for your jurisdiction rather than relying on this section number.
A shopkeeper in Coimbatore asked me about a passport being impounded or seized — what's the actual legal position under Indian law?

Before a passport can be impounded under Section 10(3), the holder is ordinarily entitled to a reasonable opportunity to be heard and to know the grounds — flowing from the Supreme Court's landmark ruling in Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978), which held that impounding a passport without a fair hearing violates the constitutional right to personal liberty. In practice, so the shopkeeper is entitled to ask for the written reasons behind the impounding order, since the passport authority is legally required to record and, in most cases, share them.
Under Indian law, what are the rules regarding getting married under the Special Marriage Act?

Section 5 of the Special Marriage Act, 1954 requires the couple to file notice with the Marriage Officer of a district where either party has resided for at least 30 days immediately before giving the notice. This residency-and-notice requirement, and the subsequent 30-day public objection window, has been criticised by courts (including remarks by the Supreme Court) as invasive of privacy, though it remains the current legal position.
A colleague at work is dealing with a situation involving maintenance for a divorced Muslim woman. What does Indian law say about this?

Under the Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Divorce) Act, 1986, if a divorced woman is unable to maintain herself even with the 'reasonable and fair provision' from her former husband, the law provides that her relatives who would inherit her property under Muslim law may be ordered to pay maintenance, and if she has no such relatives able to pay, the State Waqf Board can be directed to pay it instead. In practice, so your colleague doesn't need to accept a maintenance offer that only covers the iddat period itself — the Supreme Court's interpretation in Danial Latifi means the fair provision has to look beyond just those three months.
A friend of mine is dealing with a situation involving wife's maintenance claim. What does Indian law say about this?

Section 144 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), 2023, the successor to Section 125 CrPC, lets a wife unable to maintain herself — including a divorced wife who has not remarried — claim a monthly allowance from a husband with sufficient means who neglects or refuses to maintain her, on application before a Judicial Magistrate of the First Class.
What are the practical consequences under Indian law if the issue of the 3-month limitation to challenge an award isn't handled correctly?

Under Section 34(3) of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, a challenge to an arbitral award must be made within three months of receiving it, or of a Section 33 correction request being disposed of.
My landlord is asking for a security deposit for a ₹25,000/month residential property in a state that has adopted the Model Tenancy Act. How much can he legally demand?

Under Section 11 of the Model Tenancy Act, 2021, the security deposit a landlord can charge in advance is capped at 2 months' rent for residential premises. On a monthly rent of ₹25,000, that means the landlord cannot lawfully demand more than ₹50,000 as a security deposit. This deposit must be refunded to you by the landlord at the time you hand over vacant possession, after making any due deductions for damages or unpaid dues. Note that the Model Tenancy Act is a template law meant for states to adopt through their own legislation or rules — whether this specific cap applies to you depends on whether your state has actually enacted it or a similar rent-control framework incorporating it, so it's worth checking your state's tenancy rules to confirm this is binding rather than just persuasive guidance.
My neighbour is dealing with a situation involving notice period for agricultural or manufacturing leases. What does Indian law say about this?

Section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 treats a lease for agricultural or manufacturing purposes as a year-to-year tenancy, terminable by either the lessor or lessee giving six months' notice — a longer period than the 15 days that applies to other kinds of leases.
A client presents this factual matrix: 'A commercial client withheld cloud access keys after an invoice dispute.' Why is this information insufficient to provide definitive legal advice?

Deficiency of Facts: In Information Technology Law, this scenario lacks fundamental legal predicates: (1) The ownership clauses governing proprietary data hosted on the servers; (2) Whether the withholding constitutes unauthorized denial of access under the IT Act; (3) The dispute resolution and suspension clauses in the master services agreement. Professional Assessment: Before serving notices or instituting claims, counsel must ascertain these facts to establish limitation, proper jurisdiction, and cause of action.
How does Indian law actually treat how a correction request affects the limitation clock, and what is the specific statutory basis for it?
A genuine Section 33 correction request shifts the Section 34(3) limitation clock to run from the tribunal's disposal of that request, rather than the original award date.
A small business owner I know is dealing with a situation involving maintenance for a wife, child, or parent. What does Indian law say about this?

The maintenance provision that used to sit at CrPC Section 125 is now Section 144 of the BNSS, 2023, effective since 1 July 2024, with the substance carried over largely unchanged. Eligible claimants are a wife (including a non-remarried divorced wife), minor children, a disabled adult child, or aged parents; the person ordered to pay must have sufficient means and must have neglected or refused to maintain them. In practice, so if the other side stops paying after an order is passed, the business owner can go back to court and the Magistrate has the power to order imprisonment of up to a month for each missed payment.
How does Indian law actually treat expedited reply for life-or-liberty matters, and what is the specific statutory basis for it?
Where a request concerns information relating to the life or liberty of a person, the proviso to Section 7(1) of the RTI Act, 2005 requires a response within 48 hours.
If someone refuses to take a breathalyser test when stopped by police in Chandigarh, is that treated the same as failing it?

Yes. Under Section 185 of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988, as applied uniformly across India including in Chandigarh since this is a central law, refusal to undergo a breath test is generally treated as a positive reading for the purpose of prosecution — courts and traffic police treat refusal as an aggravating factor rather than a way to avoid the charge. If prosecuted and convicted for a first offence, the punishment is imprisonment up to 6 months, a fine up to ₹10,000, or both, with a subsequent offence attracting up to 2 years' imprisonment and a fine up to ₹15,000. The legal limit remains 30 mg of alcohol per 100 ml of blood, and beyond the breathalyser, police can rely on a blood test under Section 204 of the Act if a breath test is refused or inconclusive.
Is it true that before 2022, there was no time limit at all for filing a motor accident compensation claim in India, so people could file even after several years?

That is broadly accurate for the period before the 2019 amendment's Section 166(3) took effect. Prior to that, Section 166 of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 did not itself prescribe a strict limitation period, and courts generally took a liberal view, allowing delayed claims to be considered (sometimes applying the residuary three-year period under Article 137 of the Limitation Act, 1963 by analogy, though it was not treated as a rigid bar) given the compensatory and beneficial nature of the provision. This changed when the Motor Vehicles (Amendment) Act, 2019 inserted Section 166(3), imposing a strict six-month limitation from the date of the accident — but that provision was only notified and brought into force from 1 April 2022, not from the date the amendment was passed in 2019. That six-month rule is itself now under constitutional challenge before the Supreme Court, so the position may change again.
How do the missing details in 'My company terminated my services without paying my dues or giving reasons.' affect the calculation of limitation period?

Limitation Calculation: Under the Limitation Act and Labour and Employment Law statutes, limitation runs from specific trigger events: (1) The designation and whether you qualify as a 'workman' or managerial staff; (2) Whether statutory retrenchment rules or contractual notice apply; (3) The exact severance clauses in your appointment letter. Analysis: Without knowing the exact dates of cause of action and notice, assessing whether the claim is subsisting or barred is impossible.
What are the practical consequences under Indian law if the issue of how a correction request affects the limitation clock isn't handled correctly?
A genuine Section 33 correction request shifts the Section 34(3) limitation clock to run from the tribunal's disposal of that request, rather than the original award date.
Under Indian law, what are the rules regarding identity theft using stolen credentials?

Section 66C of the Information Technology Act, 2000 punishes fraudulently or dishonestly using another person's electronic signature, password, or other unique identification feature, with imprisonment of up to three years and a fine that may extend to Rs. 1 lakh.
For my motor insurance policy: My car accident claim documents were completed 50 days back and there's been no response from the insurer. What are my rights under IRDAI rules?

Under IRDAI's claim settlement regulations, once you have submitted all necessary documents for your motor insurance claim, the insurer must settle or reject the claim within 30 days from the date it receives your last document (this window can extend to about 45 days for some categories of claims). If the insurer delays beyond this period, it is required to pay you interest at 2% above the prevailing bank rate for each day of delay, without a separate demand from you. If your claim is stuck well past this window, you can first escalate through the insurer's internal grievance redressal mechanism, and if that doesn't resolve it, approach the Insurance Ombudsman, which handles individual policyholder disputes free of charge, or file a complaint with the consumer forum under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019.
What is the correct legal procedure a tenant I spoke with should follow regarding drawer's payment window after notice under Indian law?

After a Section 138 demand notice under the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, the drawer has 15 days to pay the cheque amount; only if payment is not made within that window does the cause of action to file a complaint arise.
A friend's mother is dealing with a situation involving anticipatory bail. What does Indian law say about this?

Under the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, the right to seek bail before arrest sits in Section 482, taking over from the old CrPC Section 438. Any person with reasonable grounds to believe they may be arrested for a non-bailable offence can move the Sessions Court or High Court for anticipatory bail — except where Section 482(4) applies, which excludes accusations of raping a minor under sixteen or gang rape of a woman under eighteen. In practice, in your friend's mother's case, this means the application has to go before the Sessions Court or High Court, not a Magistrate, and should set out concretely why arrest is apprehended.
Can you explain what Indian law says about a passport being impounded or seized, for my cousin in Pune?

An order impounding a passport under Section 10(3) of the Passports Act, 1967 can be appealed to the Central Passport Organisation (or, depending on which authority passed the order, a designated appellate authority) within 30 days of the order being communicated to the holder. In practice, for your cousin, the key question is which authority actually impounded the passport — if it was just the police holding onto it (as opposed to a formal impounding order from the passport office), that itself may be legally questionable.
I heard something about National Commission pecuniary jurisdiction that I'm not sure is accurate under Indian law — can you confirm what the actual legal position is?

Under the 2021 Jurisdiction Rules, the National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission has jurisdiction over complaints where the consideration paid for goods or services exceeds Rs. 2 crore. Note that jurisdiction under the 2019 Act is fixed by the consideration paid, not the compensation claimed, unlike the older 1986 Act.

A 16-year-and-2-month-old is accused of a heinous offence. Does the Juvenile Justice Board need to wait for a formal request before starting the preliminary assessment, or does it happen automatically?

It happens as a matter of course once the two threshold conditions are met — there's no need for anyone to formally request it. Under Section 15 of the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015, whenever a child who has completed 16 years of age (which your 16-year-2-month-old clearly has) is accused of a heinous offence as defined under Section 2(33), the Juvenile Justice Board is statutorily required to conduct the preliminary assessment itself, as part of its inquiry process under Section 14(5)(f). The Board must complete this assessment within 3 months of the child first being produced before it, examining his mental and physical capacity to have committed the offence, his ability to understand the consequences, and the circumstances of the alleged offence, using expert psychologists or psycho-social workers if needed, before deciding whether he should be tried as an adult under Section 18(3) or remain within the juvenile justice system.
In Haryana, if someone is caught drunk driving a second time after already being convicted once, what happens?

For a subsequent offence under Section 185 of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988, the punishment is more severe: imprisonment up to 2 years, a fine up to ₹15,000, or both — this applies uniformly across India, including in Haryana, since the Motor Vehicles Act is a central law. License suspension is also more likely to be for a longer duration on a repeat conviction, and courts generally treat a second conviction far more strictly than a first one, since the law's 2019 amendment specifically raised penalties to deter repeat offenders.
If a friend of mine is affected by civil liability for unauthorized computer access, what should they know about their legal rights or obligations?

Beyond the criminal liability under Section 66C of the IT Act, 2000 for identity theft, unauthorized access to a computer resource can separately attract civil liability for damages by way of compensation under Section 43 of the Act.
A party claims: 'An idea or business model can be directly patented in India.' What is the correct legal response to this assertion?

Legal Response: This assertion has no legal standing in Indian jurisprudence. Explanation: Under Section 3 of the Indian Patents Act, abstract ideas, scientific principles, business methods, and algorithms per se are not patentable. Only concrete, technical inventions with novel practical utility qualify. Advise: Reject the assertion in formal correspondence citing the applicable legal rules.
How does Indian law actually treat duty to report child sexual abuse, and what is the specific statutory basis for it?
Section 19 of the POCSO Act, 2012 places a duty on any person who has knowledge of or apprehends an offence under the Act to report it to the police or the Special Juvenile Police Unit.
A colleague at work is dealing with a situation involving police assistance in implementing an order. What does Indian law say about this?

Section 19(5) of the PWDV Act, 2005 allows the Magistrate, while passing a residence or protection order, to direct the officer-in-charge of the nearest police station to give protection to the aggrieved person or assist in implementing the order.
Can you explain what Indian law says about how long you have to file a civil suit, for a friend's mother?

The Limitation Act, 1963 prescribes different time limits depending on the type of claim — commonly three years for suits on contracts or debts, and twelve years for suits to recover possession of land. Section 6 extends this by allowing time to run from when a disability (such as minority) ends, rather than from the original date the cause of action arose, where the claimant was a minor or of unsound mind at that time. In practice, so if your friend's mother was a minor when the cause of action arose, the three-year period only starts running once they turn 18, not from the original date of the incident.
If my elder relative is affected by maternity leave entitlement, what should they know about their legal rights or obligations?

A woman is entitled to 26 weeks of paid maternity leave under the amended Maternity Benefit Act, 1961 for her first two surviving children — this can be split as up to 8 weeks before the expected delivery date and the rest after. The Act also mandates a creche facility in establishments with 50 or more employees, and permits a work-from-home arrangement after the 26-week leave ends, where the nature of the work allows it. In practice, in your elder relative's case, since this would be a third child, the entitlement is 12 weeks rather than 26, which is worth knowing before she plans her leave dates.
Under Indian law, what are the rules regarding transfers other than gifts covered by Section 23?

Section 23(1) of the Senior Citizens Act, 2007 is not limited to gifts — the phrase "transferred by way of gift or otherwise" has been read by courts to also cover release deeds, settlements, and sales made on the understanding that the senior citizen would be looked after, so such transfers can equally be challenged if the condition is breached.
Under Indian law, what are the rules regarding a 16-18 year old accused of a serious crime?

Offences under the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015 are split into petty (up to 3 years), serious (3 to 7 years), and heinous (7 years or more) categories. Only the heinous category, and only for children between 16 and 18, opens the door to trial as an adult, following a preliminary capacity assessment by the Juvenile Justice Board — a child below 16, regardless of the offence, cannot be tried as an adult under this Act.
Can you explain what Indian law says about minority shareholders being treated unfairly in a company, for a tenant I know?

The high-profile Tata Sons v. Cyrus Mistry dispute was fought under Sections 241-242 of the Companies Act, 2013 — illustrating that this remedy isn't limited to small family companies, but is available even in large public companies where minority (or removed) shareholders believe the majority's conduct has been unfairly prejudicial to their interests. In practice, for the tenant, the first practical check is the numerical threshold under Section 244 — without holding at least 10% of shares (or meeting the 100-member/one-tenth alternative), the petition to NCLT can't even be filed.
I was harmed by a gas cylinder regulator that leaked and caused a fire in my kitchen. Can I claim compensation from the manufacturer under Indian consumer law?

Yes — this falls under the product liability provisions in Chapter VI of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019. Section 84 makes a product manufacturer liable in a product liability action where, among other grounds, the product has a manufacturing defect, is defective in design, deviates from its own manufacturing specifications, doesn't conform to an express warranty, or lacks adequate instructions and warnings to prevent harm — your case appears to involve manufacturing defect combined with inadequate usage instructions. Importantly, under Section 84(2), the manufacturer can be held liable even if they weren't negligent or fraudulent in making an express warranty, which introduces a strict-liability element focused on whether the product caused harm rather than the manufacturer's intent. You can file a complaint before the relevant Consumer Commission (District, State, or National, depending on the claim value), which has the power to order removal of the defect, replacement, refund with interest, compensation including punitive damages for negligence, and even direct withdrawal of the hazardous product from the market. Keep your purchase receipt, photos or medical records of the harm, and any advertising material showing the manufacturer's claims, as this evidence strengthens a product liability claim.
I was harmed by an electric heater that caught fire despite being used exactly as instructed. Can I claim compensation from the manufacturer under Indian consumer law?

Yes — this falls under the product liability provisions in Chapter VI of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019. Section 84 makes a product manufacturer liable in a product liability action where, among other grounds, the product has a manufacturing defect, is defective in design, deviates from its own manufacturing specifications, doesn't conform to an express warranty, or lacks adequate instructions and warnings to prevent harm — your case appears to involve manufacturing defect or design defect causing the malfunction. Importantly, under Section 84(2), the manufacturer can be held liable even if they weren't negligent or fraudulent in making an express warranty, which introduces a strict-liability element focused on whether the product caused harm rather than the manufacturer's intent. You can file a complaint before the relevant Consumer Commission (District, State, or National, depending on the claim value), which has the power to order removal of the defect, replacement, refund with interest, compensation including punitive damages for negligence, and even direct withdrawal of the hazardous product from the market. Keep your purchase receipt, photos or medical records of the harm, and any advertising material showing the manufacturer's claims, as this evidence strengthens a product liability claim.

I'm Vikram. I noticed a UPI transaction I never authorised for Rs. 150000, and I reported it to my bank about 80 hours after I got the bank's SMS alert (a bit later than I'd have liked). Will I get the full amount back?

Reporting after roughly 3.3 days puts you past the 3-working-day zero-liability window (note: this is 3 WORKING days, not a flat 72 hours -- the two aren't the same measure). You may still fall in the 'limited liability' category if you reported within 4-7 working days, where your liability is capped -- typically Rs. 5,000, Rs. 10,000, or Rs. 25,000 depending on your account/card type, rather than the full Rs. 150000.

Beyond 7 working days, liability depends on the bank's own board-approved policy, so it can vary. File your complaint in writing regardless, since even outside these windows banks are required to investigate and can still credit some or all of the amount depending on the facts.
A 11-year-old has disclosed being sexually assaulted by their tuition teacher. What punishment applies?

Since the victim is 11 years old, this falls under the enhanced protection for children below 16. Under Section 4 of the POCSO Act, 2012 (as amended in 2019), penetrative sexual assault on a child below 16 carries a minimum sentence of rigorous imprisonment for 20 years, extendable to imprisonment for the remainder of the accused's natural life, plus a mandatory fine used for the victim's medical treatment and rehabilitation. Because the accused is a tuition teacher — someone in a position of trust and authority over the child — the offence likely also qualifies as aggravated penetrative sexual assault under Sections 5 and 6, which similarly carries a minimum of 20 years, extendable to life or, in the most extreme cases, the death penalty. Consent is legally irrelevant given the victim's age, and the case is tried by a Special POCSO Court.
Which court or authority has jurisdiction over seeking anticipatory bail under BNSS, and how does the process commence?

Jurisdictional Framework: Jurisdiction for seeking anticipatory bail under BNSS is determined by statutory rules under Criminal Procedure. Initial Filing: Establish reasonable apprehension of arrest in a non-bailable offence. Followed by: File an application before the Sessions Court or High Court through an advocate. Adjudication Route: Ensure advance notice to the Public Prosecutor. Concluding with: Comply strictly with conditions imposed by the court. Filing before a court lacking territorial or pecuniary jurisdiction will result in return or transfer of the petition.
What are the practical consequences under Indian law if the issue of maintenance for elderly parents isn't handled correctly?
Under Section 144 of the BNSS, 2023, a father or mother unable to maintain themselves can claim a monthly allowance from a child who has sufficient means but neglects or refuses to maintain them.
I'm buying a plot of land worth Rs. 15 lakh from a private seller through a simple sale agreement. Do we actually need to get this registered, or is a signed agreement enough to transfer ownership?

A signed agreement alone will not transfer ownership or be admissible to prove your title. Under Section 17(1)(b) of the Registration Act, 1908, any non-testamentary document that creates, assigns, limits, or extinguishes a right, title, or interest of Rs. 100 or more in immovable property must be compulsorily registered — and a plot worth Rs. 15 lakh clearly falls well within this requirement. Since the threshold is only Rs. 100 (an old, unrevised figure), in practice almost every real property sale needs registration. Under Section 49 of the Registration Act, an unregistered document that should have been registered cannot be admitted as evidence of the transaction affecting the immovable property (though it may sometimes be looked at for limited collateral purposes, such as showing the nature of someone's possession). You should execute a proper registered sale deed rather than relying on the agreement alone.
Why have Indian courts consistently rejected the premise that 'A bounced cheque is merely a civil breach with no criminal consequences.'?

Judicial Rationale: Courts reject this premise because it undermines public policy and statutory intent in Banking and Financial Law. Legal Reasoning: Under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, dishonour of a cheque for insufficiency of funds is a criminal offence punishable with imprisonment or fine up to twice the cheque amount, alongside civil recovery remedies. Precedent: Judicial orders hold that statutory mandates cannot be bypassed by customary assumptions.
What essential standards and statutory principles govern direct vs indirect tax under Indian law?

Under Tax-related legal concepts, direct vs indirect tax is governed by established statutory standards and judicial doctrines. Direct taxes like income tax are levied directly on income/wealth of a person, while indirect taxes like GST are levied on the supply of goods and services and generally passed on to the consumer. Courts and regulatory bodies require strict adherence to procedural fairness, proper documentation, and statutory preconditions before granting relief or enforcing liabilities under this principle.
Under Indian law, what are the rules regarding the second-motion cooling-off period?

Section 13B(2) of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 requires a second motion to be moved not before six months and not later than eighteen months after the first motion for mutual consent divorce, during which the court checks that consent remains genuine and the petition has not been withdrawn.
A cheque for ₹800,000 that someone gave me to repay a debt bounced due to insufficient funds. What are my legal options?

This is governed by Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881. First, you (or your lawyer) must send the drawer a written legal notice within 30 days of learning the cheque bounced, demanding payment of the ₹800,000. The drawer then has 15 days from receiving that notice to pay up; if they don't, your cause of action for filing a criminal complaint begins on the 16th day, and you generally have 1 month from then to file the complaint in the appropriate Magistrate's court (delay beyond this needs a condonation application with sufficient cause shown). If convicted, the drawer faces imprisonment up to 2 years, a fine up to twice the cheque amount (up to ₹1,600,000 here), or both — and courts often lean toward ordering payment of compensation (up to the cheque amount or more) rather than jail time, especially if the drawer is willing to pay. The offence is bailable, compoundable, and non-cognizable, meaning the matter can be settled between you and the drawer at any stage of the proceedings.
A colleague at work is dealing with a situation involving a 16-18 year old accused of a serious crime. What does Indian law say about this?

Under the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015, a child aged 16 to 18 accused of a "heinous offence" — defined under Section 2(33) as one carrying a minimum sentence of seven years or more — can be tried as an adult, but only after the Juvenile Justice Board conducts a preliminary assessment of the child's mental and physical capacity to commit the offence and their ability to understand its consequences, under Section 15. In practice, for your colleague, the age at the time of the alleged offence is critical — if the child was under 16, this adult-trial provision simply doesn't apply regardless of how serious the offence was.
How does Indian law actually treat maintenance for a disabled adult child, and what is the specific statutory basis for it?

Section 144 BNSS, 2023 also covers a legitimate or illegitimate major child who is unable to maintain itself because of a physical or mental abnormality or injury, letting such a child claim maintenance from a parent with sufficient means.
I run a small consulting business in Maharashtra with annual turnover around ₹1,800,000. Do I need to register for GST?

Under Section 22 of the Central Goods and Services Tax (CGST) Act, 2017, registration becomes mandatory once your PAN-based aggregate turnover in a financial year crosses the applicable threshold. For a supplier of services in Maharashtra, the threshold is ₹40 lakh for goods or ₹20 lakh for services, since Maharashtra follows the higher normal-category limit that applies in most Indian states. Since your turnover of ₹1,800,000 is below this ₹2,000,000 threshold, registration isn't mandatory yet, though you can opt for voluntary registration under Section 25(3) if you want to claim input tax credit or issue GST invoices. Note that certain categories — like inter-state suppliers, e-commerce sellers, or those under compulsory registration in Section 24 — must register regardless of turnover.
What legal traps or risks arise if someone relies on the assumption that 'Company directors have absolute immunity and can never be held personally liable for company defaults.'?

Risk Overview: Relying on 'Company directors have absolute immunity and can never be held personally liable for company defaults.' exposes individuals to serious legal vulnerabilities in Company and Business Law. Correct Principle: Director immunity is not absolute. Directors face personal liability for statutory tax defaults, bouncing company cheques under the NI Act, fraud, and situations where courts pierce the corporate veil. Next Step: Consult an advocate and rely exclusively on formal registered documentation and statutory procedures.
My elder relative is dealing with a situation involving anticipatory bail. What does Indian law say about this?

Anticipatory bail is now governed by Section 482 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), 2023, which replaced Section 438 of the old CrPC from 1 July 2024. It lets a person who reasonably fears arrest for a non-bailable offence apply to the Sessions Court or High Court for a direction that, if arrested, they be released on bail. Under Section 482(4), this remedy is barred for anyone accused of raping a woman under sixteen, or of gang rape of a woman under eighteen. In practice, for your elder relative, the first thing to confirm is which offence is alleged — if it falls under the Section 482(4) exception, anticipatory bail simply isn't available and a different strategy is needed.
My elderly father gave his house to my brother in writing, on the condition that my brother would take care of him. Now my brother has thrown him out. What can my father do?

Under Section 23 of the Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior Citizens Act, 2007, if a senior citizen transfers property (by gift or otherwise) on the condition that the transferee will provide basic amenities and physical needs, and the transferee then refuses or fails to do so, the transfer is deemed to have been made by fraud, coercion, or undue influence, and can be declared void at the senior citizen's option by the Maintenance Tribunal set up under the Act. Your father can approach the Tribunal (usually headed by the Sub-Divisional Magistrate/Revenue Divisional Officer in most states) with the transfer document and evidence that your brother has failed to provide the promised care, and seek to have the transfer cancelled. One point to flag: courts have taken slightly different views on whether the maintenance condition needs to be explicitly written into the transfer document -- the Madras High Court has held that an express clause is required, while the Bombay High Court more recently (2026) held that the condition can sometimes be inferred even without an express clause. So it will help your father's case significantly if the original document does clearly record that the transfer was conditional on being cared for. This is general information; he should approach a lawyer or directly the Maintenance Tribunal in your district promptly.
My sister wants to file for a protection order against her husband but doesn't know where to start. What does the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005 provide?

Under Section 12 of the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005, she (or a Protection Officer, or someone acting on her behalf) can present an application to the Magistrate seeking one or more reliefs under the Act. The Magistrate must take into account any Domestic Incident Report received from the Protection Officer or service provider before passing orders, and is required under Section 12(5) to endeavour to dispose of the application within 60 days of the first hearing.
What does the law say if my neighbour is facing a passport being impounded or seized?

Under Section 10(3) of the Passports Act, 1967, a passport can be impounded or revoked by the passport authority on specific statutory grounds — including where the passport was obtained by suppressing material facts or giving false information, or where a court has issued a warrant, summons, or an order prohibiting the holder's departure from India in a pending case. The passport authority is required to record its reasons in writing and, on demand, share a copy with the holder (unless doing so would harm India's security or foreign relations). In practice, in your neighbour's case, since the Maneka Gandhi ruling requires a fair hearing before impounding, it's worth checking whether your neighbour was actually given a chance to respond before the order was passed.
I heard that an idea or business model can be directly patented in india. Is this legally true in India?

Direct Correction: That assumption is legally incorrect under Indian law. Legal Reality: Under Section 3 of the Indian Patents Act, abstract ideas, scientific principles, business methods, and algorithms per se are not patentable. Only concrete, technical inventions with novel practical utility qualify. Practical Caution: Acting on popular misconceptions can lead to severe legal prejudice; rights must be verified under governing statutes.
How does Indian law actually treat the 3-month limitation to challenge an award, and what is the specific statutory basis for it?

Under Section 34(3) of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, a challenge to an arbitral award must be made within three months of receiving it, or of a Section 33 correction request being disposed of.
If a colleague at work is affected by a builder delaying possession of a flat, what should they know about their legal rights or obligations?

A homebuyer's remedy for delayed possession sits in Section 18 of RERA, 2016 — it isn't something that has to be separately negotiated into the sale agreement, since it's a statutory right. The choice between a refund-with-interest and monthly delay-interest belongs to the buyer, and the claim is filed before the State Real Estate Regulatory Authority, which is meant to dispose of such complaints within a set timeframe. In practice, so if the builder ignores your colleague's demand, the next step is a formal complaint to the state RERA authority, which can also penalise the builder separately for the delay.
If a friend from Chennai is affected by how long you have to file a civil suit, what should they know about their legal rights or obligations?

The Limitation Act, 1963 prescribes different time limits depending on the type of claim — commonly three years for suits on contracts or debts, and twelve years for suits to recover possession of land. Section 6 extends this by allowing time to run from when a disability (such as minority) ends, rather than from the original date the cause of action arose, where the claimant was a minor or of unsound mind at that time. In practice, so if your friend was a minor when the cause of action arose, the three-year period only starts running once they turn 18, not from the original date of the incident.
I'm Kavita. Arjun's cheque for Rs. 250000 bounced, and I sent the legal notice 14 days ago. Arjun hasn't responded. What happens now?

Since Arjun received the notice 14 days ago, they still have until the 15-day mark to make the payment. If that period passes with no payment, the offence under Section 138 NI Act is treated as complete, and you get 30 days from the end of the 15-day period to file a criminal complaint in the appropriate Magistrate's court.

Keep your proof of notice delivery (courier/postal receipt, or acknowledgment) safe, as you'll need it to show the notice was validly served. If payment does come in during the remaining days, that would resolve the matter without needing to go to court.
If a friend from Chennai is affected by anticipatory bail, what should they know about their legal rights or obligations?

Since 1 July 2024, pre-arrest (anticipatory) bail applications are filed under BNSS Section 482, not the earlier CrPC Section 438. The core protection is the same — a person apprehending arrest in a non-bailable case can approach the Sessions Court or High Court in advance — but Section 482(4) carves out an exception, denying this relief to those accused of raping a girl under sixteen or of gang-raping a woman under eighteen. In practice, so if your friend is filing this application now, it should specifically cite BNSS Section 482, since courts have been rejecting applications that are still worded under the repealed CrPC Section 438.
I'm Manoj. As a disabled adult daughter, my husband has stopped giving me any money for the last four months. Can I claim maintenance, and how does that work?

Yes -- under Section 144 of the BNSS (the successor to the old Section 125 CrPC, in force since 1 July 2024), a Magistrate can order a person with sufficient means to pay monthly maintenance if they've neglected or refused to maintain a wife, minor child, a major child unable to maintain itself due to disability, or a parent unable to maintain themselves.

To succeed, you'd generally need to show three things: the other person has sufficient means, they've neglected or refused to maintain you, and you're unable to maintain yourself. This provision applies regardless of religion. If you file an application, both sides are usually required to submit affidavits disclosing their income and assets, and courts are expected to decide interim maintenance applications within 60 days of the notice being served.
I received an arbitral award in a vendor payment dispute 3 months and 2 days ago and only just found a strong ground to challenge it. Is there any way around the deadline?

This is tight. Under Section 34(3) of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, you had 3 months from receipt of the award to file your Section 34 application, and courts can extend this by a further 30 days only on showing sufficient cause for the delay — but not beyond that additional 30 days under any circumstances, since the Supreme Court has treated this outer limit as absolute. Since you are only 2 days past the initial 3-month window, you are very likely still within the condonable 30-day extension period, so you should file immediately along with an application explaining the sufficient cause for the short delay (for instance, when you discovered the ground for challenge). Don't wait any further, since every additional day narrows your margin within that 30-day buffer.
Can you explain the current Indian legal position on setting up an Internal Committee against workplace harassment?

Under Section 4 of the POSH Act, 2013, the 10-employee threshold that triggers a mandatory Internal Committee counts everyone — permanent staff, contract workers, interns, and daily-wage employees combined. Where the workplace is below that threshold, the complaint is instead handled by the district-level Local Committee. Section 26 of the Act penalises an employer's failure to constitute the IC, with fines starting at Rs 50,000.
My cousin who works in chennai is dealing with a situation involving bond to prevent further violence. What does Indian law say about this?

Under Section 19(3) of the PWDV Act, 2005, the Magistrate may require the respondent to execute a bond, with or without sureties, to prevent the commission of further domestic violence; such an order is treated as one under Chapter VIII of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 for enforcement purposes.
If my cousin who works in Chennai is affected by the 30-day condonable extension, what should they know about their legal rights or obligations?

The proviso to Section 34(3) of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 allows the court to entertain a delayed challenge to an arbitral award for a further 30 days beyond the three-month limitation period if sufficient cause is shown — but the words "not thereafter" make this an absolute outer limit that courts, including the Supreme Court, have applied strictly.
A builder in Thiruvananthapuram changed my flat's possession date without my consent, and I paid ₹8,200,000 so far. Can I get out of the deal?

Yes. Under Section 18(1) of the Real Estate (Regulation and Development) Act, 2016, if the builder unilaterally changes the agreed possession date, you have the right to withdraw from the project. You must exercise this within 45 days of the changed date being communicated (or of the original committed date passing without possession), and on withdrawal, the builder is required to refund the full ₹8,200,000 you've paid, along with interest at the rate notified by the Thiruvananthapuram state's RERA authority. Alternatively, instead of withdrawing, you can choose to remain in the project and claim monthly interest compensation for the delay until possession is actually handed over. Either way, you should file your complaint with the relevant state RERA authority to enforce this right, since the builder is unlikely to volunteer the refund without a formal demand or complaint.
Can you explain what Indian law says about setting up an Internal Committee against workplace harassment, for a small business owner I know?

Any workplace in India — private, government, NGO, or otherwise — with 10 or more employees must have an Internal Committee under Section 4 of the POSH Act, 2013, with at least half its members being women and one external member from outside the organisation. Employers who don't comply can be fined starting at Rs 50,000 under Section 26, with the penalty doubling on a second violation. In practice, in the business owner's case, if the workplace has fewer than 10 employees, the complaint should go to the district's Local Committee instead of expecting an internal process.
Someone I met recently is dealing with a situation involving being laid off or retrenched from a job. What does Indian law say about this?

The Industrial Disputes Act's retrenchment compensation under Section 25F is calculated the same way as gratuity — 15 days' average pay for every completed year of continuous service (or part thereof exceeding six months) — but it's a separate entitlement from gratuity, payable in addition to it where both apply, and gratuity payable on retrenchment is specifically excluded from the retrenchment compensation calculation itself. In practice, so if this person's job ended because the whole business was sold or transferred, the same notice-and-compensation protection applies unless the new employer kept this person on with no less favourable terms.
A colleague at work is dealing with a situation involving notice must align with the tenancy cycle. What does Indian law say about this?

A 15-day termination notice for a month-to-month tenancy under Section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 should be structured to expire with the end of a month of the tenancy — aligned with the monthly rental cycle — rather than being calculated as an arbitrary count of 15 calendar days from any date.
What is the hierarchy of appeals available to an aggrieved party in Education-related law?

Appellate Hierarchy: In Education-related law, initial orders from statutory tribunals or trial courts are subject to structured appeals. Statutory Appeal: First appeals generally lie on questions of fact and law to the immediate appellate authority or District/High Court. Subsequent Review: Second appeals or revisions are typically restricted to substantial questions of law, concluding with discretionary review under Article 136 of the Constitution.
What is the correct legal procedure a classmate studying law should follow regarding police assistance in implementing an order under Indian law?
Section 19(5) of the PWDV Act, 2005 lets the Magistrate direct the local police officer-in-charge to assist in implementing a residence or protection order.
A 16-year-old is accused of kidnapping for ransom, a heinous offence. Will the Juvenile Justice Board automatically send him for adult trial?

No, not automatically. Kidnapping for ransom typically qualifies as a 'heinous offence' under Section 2(33) of the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015, since it usually carries a minimum sentence of 7 years or more. But because he has completed 16 years, Section 15 requires the Board to first conduct a preliminary assessment of his mental and physical capacity to have committed the offence, his ability to understand its consequences, and the surrounding circumstances, using expert psychologists or psycho-social workers if needed, to be completed within 3 months of his first production before the Board. Only if the Board concludes he should be tried as an adult does it pass an order under Section 18(3) sending the case to the Children's Court; otherwise the matter is handled by the Board itself under the juvenile system.
A friend from Chennai asked me about how long a trademark registration lasts — what's the actual legal position under Indian law?

The 10-year validity clock for an Indian trademark under Section 25 of the Trade Marks Act, 1999 runs from the original filing date, even if the actual registration certificate takes a couple of years to be issued due to examination or opposition — so a mark filed in 2020 that gets registered only in 2022 is still due for renewal in 2030, not 2032. In practice, so if your friend registered the mark but hasn't actually been using it in business for five years since registration, that's a separate vulnerability the Registrar can act on, quite apart from the renewal question.
Under Indian law, what are the rules regarding notice period for agricultural or manufacturing leases?

Section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 treats a lease for agricultural or manufacturing purposes as a year-to-year tenancy, terminable by either the lessor or lessee giving six months' notice — a longer period than the 15 days that applies to other kinds of leases.
Under Indian law, what are the rules regarding a daughter's coparcenary rights?

A daughter's right to be treated as a coparcener — entitled to an equal share in ancestral Mitakshara property, same as a son — flows from the amended Section 6 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, in force since 9 September 2005. The Supreme Court settled the scope of this right in Vineeta Sharma v. Rakesh Sharma (2020), holding it applies irrespective of whether the father was alive on that date, provided the daughter herself was.
A drone I bought malfunctioned mid-flight due to a firmware defect and crashed into my neighbour's car. Who is liable — me, the seller, or the manufacturer?

Under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019's product liability provisions, primary liability for a firmware or manufacturing defect generally falls on the product manufacturer under Section 84, since the defect originated in how the product was made or designed rather than anything you did as the user. Your neighbour, as the injured third party, could potentially bring a claim as well, since product liability actions aren't limited only to the direct purchaser — anyone who suffers harm from the defective product may have a claim. The seller could also face liability under Section 86 in certain circumstances, such as if they exercised substantial control over the product's design or manufacturing, or made an independent warranty. As the purchaser, you would generally not be personally liable for a defect that existed in the product when you bought it, though your neighbour may still approach you first since you were the immediate operator, and you could then seek to bring the manufacturer into the proceedings or pursue your own claim against them.
If a person I met recently is affected by bond to prevent further violence, what should they know about their legal rights or obligations?

Under Section 19(3) of the PWDV Act, 2005, the Magistrate may require the respondent to execute a bond, with or without sureties, to prevent the commission of further domestic violence; such an order is treated as one under Chapter VIII of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 for enforcement purposes.
A child aged 12 has disclosed being sexually assaulted by a relative. What punishment does Indian law prescribe for the accused?

Under Section 4 of the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences (POCSO) Act, 2012, as amended in 2019, penetrative sexual assault on a child below 16 years of age — which covers a 12-year-old victim — carries a minimum sentence of rigorous imprisonment for 20 years, extendable to imprisonment for the remainder of the accused's natural life, along with a mandatory fine. The 2019 amendment specifically raised this minimum from 10 to 20 years for victims under 16 to reflect the heightened severity. Since the accused is described as a relative, the offence may also qualify as aggravated penetrative sexual assault under Section 5/6 if the relative was in a position of trust or authority, in which case the minimum sentence rises further to 20 years up to life, or even the death penalty in the most extreme cases where the court considers it warranted. Since a child under 18 is involved, consent is legally irrelevant, and the case will be tried by a Special POCSO Court, with the trial conducted in a manner sensitive to the child.
What are the sequential procedural steps for registering an FIR under Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS) in India?

The process for registering an FIR under Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS) under Criminal Procedure requires compliance with established steps: Step 1: Report the cognizable offence to the police station having jurisdiction, or register a Zero FIR if urgent. Step 2: Ensure the statement is reduced to writing and read back to you. Step 3: Obtain an authenticated copy of the registered FIR free of cost. Step 4: If refused, escalate in writing to the Superintendent of Police or Magistrate. Formats, fee schedules, and limitation periods must be verified with the official forum rules.
Can you explain what Indian law says about whether a small business needs to register for GST, for a factory worker I spoke with?

Certain categories of suppliers must register for GST from day one, irrespective of turnover — this includes anyone making inter-state taxable supplies, e-commerce operators, and casual taxable persons, among others. For everyone else, the general goods/services turnover thresholds (currently Rs 40 lakh / Rs 20 lakh in most states) determine when registration becomes compulsory. In practice, for the worker, the calculation needs to include all supplies — even exempt sales and any inter-state supply — not just the obviously taxable revenue, since 'aggregate turnover' is defined more broadly than that.
What is the correct legal procedure someone from my hometown should follow regarding how a correction request affects the limitation clock under Indian law?
A genuine Section 33 correction request shifts the Section 34(3) limitation clock to run from the tribunal's disposal of that request, rather than the original award date.
If someone in my family is affected by eligibility for mutual consent divorce, what should they know about their legal rights or obligations?

Section 13B(1) of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 allows both spouses to file a joint petition for divorce by mutual consent if they have lived separately for at least one year, cannot live together, and mutually agree the marriage should be dissolved.

I'm Ramesh. I was in a road accident 10 year(s) ago that caused the loss of my father in the accident, and I never filed for compensation. Is it too late to approach the Motor Accidents Claims Tribunal?

You're likely not barred by time. Unlike many other claims, there's no fixed limitation period for filing a compensation claim before the Motor Accidents Claims Tribunal (MACT) -- an older six-month bar under a earlier provision was removed by amendment. That said, a delay of 10 year(s) is fairly long, and the Tribunal can still ask you to explain the delay even though there's no statutory deadline forcing rejection.

Practical point: gather whatever records you still have -- the FIR, medical/post-mortem records, hospital bills, and any accident report -- since after this much time, evidence becomes harder to establish. I'd recommend approaching a lawyer soon to file the claim rather than delaying further, given how documentation degrades over time.
